title: Ambient noise tomography images accreted terranes and igneous provinces in Hispaniola and Puerto Rico
authors: Diego A Quiros and J Pulliam and D Barman and E Polanco Rivera and V Huerfano
abstract: The North American‐Caribbean plate boundary near the islands of Hispaniola and Puerto Rico is a complex region in which strain is accommodated by different modes of deformation. In 2013, 16 broadband stations were deployed in the Dominican Republic to densify the local permanent network. One goal is to combine their data with those from permanent networks in the Caribbean to develop a better understanding of the crust and upper mantle structure in the Greater Antilles. Here we use the records of 204 stations spanning almost 7 years of data to obtain group velocity maps. We observe at short periods the contacts between accreted terranes and the igneous provinces of Hispaniola and Puerto Rico, at longer periods the collisional boundary between the buoyant Bahamas Carbonate Platform and Hispaniola, and the transition from Hispaniola's accreted terranes to the faster lithosphere of the Venezuelan …

title: An optimized finite-difference method to minimize numerical dispersion of acoustic wave propagation using a genetic algorithm
authors: Mounika Vanga and Debajeet Barman and Maheswar Ojha
abstract: The finite-difference method (FDM) is one of the most popular methods for numerical simulation of wave propagation. The major challenge that we face in solving a partial differential equation for the wave propagation is numerical dispersion. We use an automated and optimized FDM using a genetic algorithm (GA) to optimally compute second-order spatial derivatives. In our method, the explicit finite-difference coefficients are calculated using the GA to minimize the dispersion (phase velocity) for all wavenumbers without using any specific window function. The amplitudes of the pseudospectral window (finite difference [FD] coefficients) are optimized by making the phase velocity close to the analytical solution at each wavenumber and stability close to that of the conventional FDM. Although FD coefficients in this method depend on velocity, grid spacing, and time step, less dispersive solutions can be achieved …

title: Ambient seismic noise tomography of the Suwannee suture zone using cross-coherence interferometry and double beamforming
authors: Debajeet Barman and Jay Pulliam and Diego A Quiros
abstract: We use continuous data from more than 200 vertical-component broad-band seismic stations for the years 2012 and 2013 to model the crustal and lithospheric structure of the southeastern United States (SEUS). Seismic interferometry via cross-coherence is used to retrieve the surface wave Empirical Green's function (EGF) between station pairs. We mitigate the problem of non-stationary sources contributing to the extracted EGF by applying double beamforming to pairs of subarrays of stations. The recovered Rayleigh waves are used to compute group velocity dispersion maps which are then inverted to find shear wave velocity profiles using a Markov Chain Monte Carlo technique. EGFs are computed for more than 80 000 station pairs after filtering to the period band 7–60 s. title: Seismic inversion with dictionary learning using unsupervised machine learning
authors: Debajeet Barman and Mrinal K Sen
abstract: Machine Learning (ML) has recently gained immense popularity in almost every field. This popularity is attributed to the invention of the Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). A typical CNN consists of deep convolutional layers of filter, which decomposes the information into simpler forms. These filters are optimized during training with input-output pairs. During the network’s training, the network develops an abstract relationship between the output and the corresponding input. In the work, we cast the basis pursuit inversion framework in a machine learning set up. Input seismic traces are decomposed into features by a CNN that are used to represent the coefficients and the dipole dictionary. The output of the network is reconstructed to produce a reflectivity series that is convolved with a wavelet to compute a predicted trace. title: Understanding the encoder-decoder network for solving an unsupervised seismic inversion problem
authors: D Barman and R Biswas and Mrinal K Sen
abstract: Machine Learning (ML) has recently gained immense popularity in almost every field. This popularity has been mainly contributed from the success of Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) in highly non-linear complex problems. A typical CNN consists of a set of deep convolutional layers of filter, which break the information into simpler forms. These filters are optimized during training with input-output pairs. During the training of the network, the network develops an abstract relationship between the output and the corresponding input. The training of the network requires an enormous amount of input-output pairs covering different cases to generalize the predictions. However, generating these pairs can be difficult. title: High-resolution Rayleigh wave phase velocity and group velocity inversion at Sweetwater Texas using a Double Optimized MUSIC (DOPMUSIC) algorithm
abstract: Variations in crustal structure in the vicinity of the Abilene gravity minimum, north-central Texas, can be imaged via passive seismic interferometry using continuous seismic data from several Large-N nodal deployments. In this study we have three objectives: 1) Construct a phase and group velocity maps that correlate well with area's lithology, 2) evaluate the potential of the Optimized Multiple Signal Characterization (OPMUSIC) algorithm to improve resolution of the upper crust and sediments using ambient noise data, and 3) compare the performance of OPMUSIC to that of Double Beamforming (DBF) and conventional techniques.

title: High-resolution Rayleigh wave phase velocity inversion for the southeastern United States using the MUSIC algorithm
abstract: Understanding the relationships between the Gondwanan Suwannee terrane (SWT), the Laurentian continental margin, and other neighboring terranes is essential to deciphering the history of the late Paleozoic accretionary history of Laurentia, the Alleghanian orogeny, and the breakup of Pangaea. The objectives of our study are to 1) identify the terrane boundaries accurately by constructing accurate Rayleigh wave and Vs models of this region and 2) evaluate the potential of the" Multiple Signal Classification"(MUSIC) algorithm for Angle of Arrival estimation in Python and compare it with previous results obtained with Double Beamforming (DBF) which helps to correct the travel time of the wave. title: Improved shear wave velocity model of the southeastern United States from ambient noise tomography using cross-coherence interferometry
authors: Debajeet Barman and Jay Pulliam and Diego Quiros
abstract: Previous studies suggest that Laurentia moved west-northwest during Proterozoic rifting, creating a passive continental margin that consisted of distinct north-northeast-striking rift segments and east-southeast-striking transform segments, and that the opening of the Gulf of Mexico opened through a net counter-clockwise rotation of the Yucatan block. The central Gulf of Mexico coastal plain overlies the proposed Alabama-Oklahoma transform segment of the Precambrian margin but, until recently, few data constrained the margin's structure. EarthScope's USArray provides a great deal of new data with which to model crustal and lithospheric structure in the southern US This study addresses the problem of non-stationary phases during cross-correlation to extract the Rayleigh waves from ambient noise.

title: Shear wave velocity model of the southeastern United States from ambient noise tomography with double beamforming
authors: Debajeet Barman and Diego Quiros and Jay Pulliam

title: Improved Rayleigh wave group velocity estimates across the southeastern United States via double beamforming
authors: Debajeet Barman and Jay Pulliam and Diego Quiros
abstract: Characterizing the relationship between the Gondwanan Suwannee terrane (SWT), adjacent terranes, and the Laurentian continental margin in the southeastern portion of North America is critical to understanding the late Paleozoic accretionary formation history of Laurentia, the tectonics of the Alleghanian orogeny, and the nature of the breakup of Pangaea. In this study we have two goals: 1) Identify the boundaries between terranes by developing an accurate S-wave velocity model for the region and 2) evaluate the potential for double beamforming (DBF) to improve estimates of Rayleigh wave group velocity dispersion with ambient noise.

title: New Two Steps Finite Difference Scheme for Acoustic Wave Equation Using Sampling Theorem to Minimize Grid Dispersion
abstract: New two steps finite difference scheme for acoustic wave equation using sampling theorem to minimize numerical grid dispersionDebajeet Barman and MaheswarOjhaNational Geophysical Research Institute, Hyderabad, IndiaFinite difference method is widely used in seismic waveform modeling, inversion and imaging.
